# Light-Based Therapies in Aesthetic Medicine: Evidence for Photoaging, Brightening, and Hyperpigmentation Through 2026

Current evidence supports laser and IPL treatment for selected forms of photoaging and focal pigmentation, but their roles are indication-specific rather than interchangeable. Pigment-selective lasers generally provide the most direct and rapid treatment for discrete solar lentigines, while fractional lasers and IPL can address broader combinations of pigmentation, erythema, texture, and wrinkles. Melasma may improve with carefully selected laser or combination protocols, but relapse is common and treatment should remain adjunctive to rigorous photoprotection and, usually, topical or systemic therapy. LED and photobiomodulation have credible but generally modest evidence for photoaging; they are not established treatments for melasma or generalized hyperpigmentation. No supplied clinical evidence supports generalized facial “skin whitening.”

The clinically defensible terminology is targeted tone evening, reduction of visible dyschromia, restoration toward the patient’s natural color, or clearance of a defined lesion. The American Academy of Dermatology describes the goals of melasma treatment as reducing pigment production and evening skin tone back to the patient’s natural color, not changing overall constitutional skin color ([AAD melasma guidance](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/a-z/melasma-treatment)).

This review first defines the relevant conditions and evidence standards. It then catalogs laser, IPL, and LED applications, examines recent technological advances from 2020 through 2026, separates solar lentigines from melasma, and compares the modalities on efficacy, speed, durability, downtime, phototype suitability, and safety. The final sections address combination protocols, personalization, adverse effects, regulatory and ethical limits, and the gaps that prevent a universal treatment ranking.

## Scope, terminology, and evidence context

### What the treatments are intended to change

“Photoaging” refers to visible and structural changes caused largely by cumulative ultraviolet and visible-light exposure. Clinically relevant endpoints include fine and coarse wrinkles, roughness, enlarged pores, laxity, mottled pigmentation, erythema, and loss of dermal density or elasticity. A treatment that improves a wrinkle index or texture score has demonstrated improvement in that measured feature; it has not necessarily restored all components of photodamaged skin.

“Solar lentigines,” often called age spots or sun spots, are discrete, usually well-demarcated epidermal macules on chronically sun-exposed skin. They are fundamentally different from melasma. Their pigment is usually more superficial and localized, making selective pigment targeting especially relevant. Nevertheless, a clinically brown macule can resemble pigmented actinic keratosis, seborrheic keratosis, lichen planus-like keratosis, or lentigo maligna. Cosmetic treatment should follow diagnostic assessment rather than replace it. The 2026 report on a 532-nm green laser excluded equivocal lesions and considered biopsy when dermoscopy could not establish a benign diagnosis ([Zappia et al., 2026, 532-nm green laser case series and review](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9284/13/3/128)).

“Melasma” is a chronic, relapsing disorder characterized by facial patches of excess pigmentation, commonly involving the forehead, cheeks, nose, and upper lip. Its biology includes melanocyte hyperactivity, epidermal and dermal melanin, pigmentary incontinence, basement-membrane disruption, vascular changes, inflammation, hormonal influences, oxidative stress, and photoaging. The disease is especially common in Fitzpatrick phototypes III–VI and is not simply a superficial deposit that can be permanently removed in one session. A recent review emphasizes that relapse, heterogeneous disease subtypes, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), and inconsistent adherence limit durability ([Targeting Melasma review, 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12783984/)).

“Post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation” (PIH) is pigmentation that follows inflammation or injury, including acne, dermatitis, burns, or energy-based treatment. It is both a treatment target and a major treatment complication. A laser that reduces pre-existing PIH but causes new PIH may provide little net benefit, especially in darker phototypes.

“Brightening” is a useful clinical term only when it is tied to a defined endpoint. It may mean reduced lesion contrast, more even chromametric measurements, reduced melanin index, less erythema, or natural-color restoration. It should not be used to imply generalized bleaching of healthy skin.

| Clinical term | Common objective endpoints | What the endpoint does not prove |
|---|---|---|
| Photoaging | Wrinkle volume or count, roughness, pore area, elasticity, dermal density, VISIA indices, histologic collagen or elastin changes | Complete reversal of intrinsic or extrinsic aging |
| Solar lentigines | Lesion clearance, colorimetry, CIELAB L* change, blinded improvement score, dermoscopic disappearance | Permanent prevention of new lesions or recurrence |
| Melasma | MASI or modified MASI, melanin index, chromametry, VISIA pigment index, physician or patient global assessment | Permanent remission, absence of relapse, or superiority across all phototypes |
| PIH | Change in lesion area, color or melanin index, blinded photographic scoring | Safety against future treatment-induced pigmentation |
| Brightening | Tone homogeneity, reduced mottled pigmentation, restored natural color, reduced erythema | Generalized skin whitening or a change in baseline constitutional skin color |

### Modality definitions

Lasers emit relatively narrow, coherent wavelengths and permit control over pulse duration, fluence, spot size, fractional density, and treatment geometry. Depending on the wavelength and pulse, they may act through selective photothermolysis, photomechanical pigment fragmentation, laser-induced optical breakdown, or controlled thermal remodeling.

IPL is not a laser. It emits a broad, noncoherent spectrum, usually approximately 500–1200 nm, from which cutoff filters select a clinically useful range. Melanin, oxyhemoglobin, and water-related tissue effects can therefore be addressed in one treatment, but the same breadth makes parameter selection and phototype adjustment particularly important.

LED photobiomodulation (PBM) uses low-irradiance visible or near-infrared light without intentional tissue ablation or substantial thermal injury. Red and near-infrared wavelengths are primarily used for cellular and regenerative effects. The clinical dose depends on wavelength, irradiance, fluence, exposure time, distance, device geometry, and repetition. These variables are incompletely standardized.

### Evidence context and skin phototype

The strongest evidence is not evenly distributed across indications. Direct randomized comparisons exist for some laser pairs and for selected combination protocols, but no standardized head-to-head trial comparing laser, IPL, and LED for the same indication, using the same population, treatment schedule, objective endpoint, and follow-up, was retrieved. Relative rankings across modalities must therefore be treated as cross-study impressions rather than definitive comparative efficacy.

The evidence is also concentrated in Fitzpatrick III–V, particularly East Asian cohorts. The 2026 review of 1550- and 1927-nm nonablative fractional lasers included 15 studies, but approximately 79% of the 360 participants were Asian and classified as Fitzpatrick III–IV; only 29 participants were Fitzpatrick V and 9 were Fitzpatrick VI. The review concluded that the dual system is clinically established mainly for Fitzpatrick III–IV and that evidence for Fitzpatrick VI and for 1927-nm treatment remains limited ([1550/1927-nm review in skin of color](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12997386/)).

Phototype is not merely a demographic descriptor. Melanin absorbs much of the 250–1200-nm range, and darker epidermis can compete with the intended target chromophore. Greater melanocyte reactivity also increases the risk that inflammation will produce PIH. A retrospective analysis of 961 sessions of a 1550-nm erbium laser in 422 individuals reported PIH rates of 0.26% for Fitzpatrick II, 2.6% for III, 11.6% for IV, and 33% for V. These values are not universal device risks, but they illustrate why fluence, density, overlap, cooling, and aftercare cannot be separated from the modality itself ([1550/1927-nm review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12997386/)).

For all three modalities, treatment should be interpreted against photoprotection. The melasma trials that reported sustained improvement generally required frequent broad-spectrum sunscreen use and behavioral sun avoidance. A 2026 review of photoprotection summarized evidence that tinted, iron-oxide-containing sunscreen can reduce melasma relapse more effectively than a colorless formula, although protection against short-wavelength visible light remains formulation-dependent and incomplete ([Azevedo, Lorigo, and Cairrao, 2026](https://doi.org/10.3390/cimb48090921)).

## Laser therapies: current applications and recent advances

### How laser effects are produced

Selective photothermolysis uses wavelength and pulse duration to concentrate energy in a target chromophore while limiting collateral injury. In superficial pigmentation, 532 nm is strongly absorbed by melanin and can fragment or thermally damage melanin-containing structures. Picosecond pulses concentrate energy into a shorter interval and favor photomechanical effects, including pigment fragmentation and, with microlens arrays, laser-induced optical breakdown. Nanosecond Q-switched pulses also target pigment selectively but produce more thermal interaction than picosecond pulses.

Longer wavelengths such as 1064 nm penetrate more deeply and are less strongly absorbed by epidermal melanin than 532 or 755 nm. This can be useful for dermal or mixed pigmentation, but low-fluence “laser toning” requires repeated treatments and can produce mottled hypopigmentation or rebound pigmentation if parameters are excessive or poorly controlled.

Nonablative fractional lasers create microscopic treatment zones while leaving intervening skin intact. A 1550-nm erbium glass laser and a 1927-nm thulium laser primarily target water rather than melanin. The 1550-nm wavelength reaches deeper dermal tissue and is used for remodeling, scars, and some dyschromia; 1927 nm is more strongly absorbed by water and acts more superficially, making it useful for epidermal and superficial dermal pigmentation and photoaging.

Ablative fractional CO2 or Er:YAG lasers remove or vaporize columns of tissue. They can deliver stronger remodeling and facilitate topical delivery, but produce more epidermal injury, inflammation, downtime, and pigmentary risk than nonablative fractional systems.

### Laser modality catalog

Evidence is strongest for short-term lesion improvement, not recurrence prevention |

| 1064-nm Q-switched, picosecond, or microsecond Nd:YAG | Low-fluence subcellular pigment disruption; picosecond optical breakdown; microsecond thermal vascular and remodeling effects | Melasma, photoaging, dermal or mixed pigmentation, vascular-inflammatory components | Three-session picosecond treatment improved melasma at 24 weeks; dual low-fluence plus microsecond treatment required 5–10 sessions and had 12-month follow-up | Widely used but relapse-prone; parameter and cumulative-treatment effects are central |
