### Pigment-selective lasers for solar lentigines and focal dyschromia

The clearest laser application in the supplied evidence is the treatment of discrete solar lentigines. In a prospective randomized split-face trial, 20 Korean women with Fitzpatrick III–V skin received one 532-nm picosecond treatment on one side and one 532-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG treatment on the other. The picosecond protocol used 450 ps, 0.3–0.5 J/cm², a 3–4-mm spot, and 2 Hz; the Q-switched protocol used 10 ns, 0.6–0.8 J/cm², the same spot range, and 2 Hz. At 12 weeks, blinded quartile improvement scores were 2.95 for picosecond treatment and 1.8 for Q-switched treatment. PIH occurred in 5% of picosecond-treated sides and 30% of Q-switched-treated sides, although the PIH comparison did not reach statistical significance at p=0.057. Both methods were effective; the trial supports a short-term efficacy and tolerability advantage for picosecond delivery, not proof of permanent clearance ([Kim et al., 2021, 532-nm picosecond versus Q-switched laser](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7992642/)).

The study illustrates why “whitening” is a misleading description. The treatment endpoint was slight whitening of individual lentigines, and the measured result was lesion improvement on a quartile scale. It was not generalized lightening of the surrounding face.

A 2026 Italian case series described a longer-pulsed 532-nm green laser in five patients with one solar lentigo each. All five lesions were classified as complete responses at day 21, with a mean satisfaction score of 8.6/10 and erythema resolving within the first day. The protocol used a 1-mm spot, 16–18 J/cm², 16–18 ms, and one pass with minimal overlap. The result is technically useful because it reports a reproducible protocol and dermoscopic triage, but it cannot establish durable clearance: follow-up was only 21 days, with recurrence, delayed PIH, and later adverse events unmeasured ([Zappia et al., 2026](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9284/13/3/128)).

The same review places the longer-pulsed approach in context. Older comparative evidence suggests that longer-pulse 532-nm platforms can improve lentigines, but no clinical study establishes their superiority over Q-switched or picosecond systems. Device family, pulse width, fluence, overlap, endpoint intensity, phototype, and aftercare all contribute to the outcome. Aggressive immediate whitening can increase PIH without a clear efficacy advantage, supporting conservative endpoints in darker skin.

A 2026 retrospective comparison of 730-nm picosecond treatment with 532-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG included 131 adults with three different diagnoses: melasma, n=42; solar lentigines, n=60; and PIH, n=29. The 730-nm group had a lower mean post-treatment pigmentation score, 2.55±1.11 versus 3.80±1.40, and a higher reported improvement rate, 56%±10% versus 38%±8%. Adjusted odds of the study’s composite success endpoint were 4.85, with a 95% confidence interval of 2.51–9.38. However, this was retrospective, the groups received different wavelengths and pulse durations, and the source reports inconsistent 730-nm pulse and fluence ranges in different sections. It therefore supports 730 nm as promising, not as proof that the wavelength or picosecond pulse alone caused the difference ([730-nm versus 532-nm comparison](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40001-026-04099-0)).

For PIH and darker skin, low-energy 1927-nm fractional treatment offers a different strategy. A retrospective photographic review of 61 people with Fitzpatrick IV–VI treated with 5 mJ, 140-μm spots, 170-μm depth, and 5% coverage reported a mean improvement of 43.24% assessed by two independent dermatologists, without reported side effects. The endpoint was facial PIH rather than solar-lentigine-specific clearance, and long-term durability was not reported ([Garg et al. review of laser therapies in skin of color](https://doi.org/10.3390/jcm13072116)).

### 1064-nm lasers for melasma, vascular components, and photoaging

Low-fluence 1064-nm Q-switched Nd:YAG treatment, commonly called laser toning, is widely used in Asian aesthetic practice for melasma. It typically uses large spots, low fluence, multiple passes, and repeated sessions. The intended mechanism is subcellular disruption of melanosomes with limited injury to melanocytes, but the margin between useful pigment reduction and melanocyte damage is narrow.

A prospective randomized assessor-blinded Beijing trial compared three sessions of nonfractional 1064-nm picosecond Nd:YAG, three sessions of nonfractional 755-nm picosecond alexandrite, and twice-daily 2% hydroquinone for 12 weeks. Fifty-nine participants were analyzed: 20 in the 1064-nm group, 20 in the 755-nm group, and 19 in the hydroquinone group. Participants were women with Fitzpatrick III–IV skin. At week 24, four months after the final laser session, MASI improvement was 35.9% for 1064 nm, 25.5% for 755 nm, and 24.0% for hydroquinone. The 1064-nm treatment significantly outperformed both comparators, whereas 755 nm and hydroquinone were comparable ([Liang et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2023.1132823)).

The study’s recurrence findings are more clinically important than the short-term ranking. Recurrence occurred in 4 of 59 participants overall: 5.0% in the 1064-nm group, 10.0% in the 755-nm group, and 5.3% in the hydroquinone group. PIH occurred in approximately 5% of each group and resolved spontaneously within one to six months. All participants applied SPF 48, PA+++ sunscreen at 2 mg/cm² every two hours and used sun-avoidance measures. Thus, the six-month maintenance cannot be attributed to the laser alone. The trial excluded pregnancy, lactation, photosensitive disease, active melasma, recent laser or IPL, recent bleaching products, and inability to follow strict sun protection. It represents a selected, closely supervised population rather than all melasma patients.

A newer dual-mode approach combines low-fluence Q-switched 1064 nm with a 250-μs microsecond 1064-nm mode. The proposed rationale is to address melanin, superficial vascular inflammation, erythema, dermal heating, collagen remodeling, and solar elastosis rather than pigment alone. In a prospective evaluator-blinded split-face trial, 28 Chinese patients were enrolled and 21 completed five to ten monthly sessions. Participants included Fitzpatrick III, IV, and V skin.

At three months after treatment, relapse was 4.8% on the combined side versus 23.8% with low-fluence Q-switched treatment alone, p=0.047. That apparent advantage did not persist: relapse was 23.8% versus 28.6% at six months and 52.4% versus 57.1% at 12 months. MASI improved at one and three months but not significantly at six and 12 months. VISIA pigment indices improved bilaterally, with no significant treatment-side advantage, while the combined side had better red-area indices at one and six months. No treatment-related edema, blistering, PIH, hypopigmentation, infection, or scarring was reported. The appropriate interpretation is a possible short-term benefit for vascular-inflammatory components, not a demonstrated long-term anti-relapse treatment ([dual-mode LFQS plus MPW trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12241506/)).

### Nonablative fractional 1550- and 1927-nm lasers

The dual 1550/1927-nm platform is one of the most clinically developed recent technologies for resurfacing and dyschromia in skin of color. The 1550-nm erbium glass wavelength creates dermal microscopic treatment zones and stimulates remodeling; 1927-nm thulium is more strongly absorbed by water and is used for superficial pigment, actinic change, and photoaging. The system reviewed in the United States is described as approved for 1550-nm resurfacing and dyschromia including lentigines and melasma, and for 1927-nm treatment of pigmented lesions including age spots, sunspots, and ephelides. Regulatory indications are jurisdiction-specific and do not by themselves establish effectiveness.

Across 15 studies in Fitzpatrick III–VI, the 1550-nm wavelength consistently improved scarring and melasma, while 1927 nm improved melasma and photoaging. Histologic studies reported increased type I and III collagen, elastic fibers, and hyaluronic acid, as well as reduced melanin. However, biopsy samples were often very small, sometimes only two, three, or 12 participants, so histologic remodeling should not be equated with a validated clinical collagen increase in every patient ([1550/1927-nm review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12997386/)).

The 1550-nm and 1927-nm wavelengths are not risk-free in darker skin. Lower energy and density were associated with fewer PIH events in studies that directly compared settings. The review’s practical conclusion is that lower coverage, individualized microscopic-treatment-zone density, cooling, and more sessions at lower intensity may provide a safer therapeutic window than a single aggressive treatment.

A randomized study of a nonablative fractional 1927-nm diode laser included 40 adults with moderate-to-severe facial hyperpigmentation and Fitzpatrick III–V skin. Four laser treatments were given at two-week intervals, followed by assessments four and 12 weeks after the last treatment. The Mottled Pigmentation Area and Severity Index improved by approximately 50% at both follow-ups. The comparator was daily 2% hydroquinone or moisturizer, not an untreated control; both comparator groups also showed approximately 50% improvement, and hydroquinone produced better investigator-rated GAIS at week 12. The study supports improvement of facial hyperpigmentation and photodamage, not an age-spot-specific clearance rate or generalized whitening ([Vanaman Wilson et al.](https://doi.org/10.1097/dss.0000000000001521)).

The 2025 systematic review of 1927-nm thulium treatment included 17 studies and 448 participants with various dermatologic conditions. Average protocols involved three sessions at monthly intervals and approximately 120 days of follow-up. Improvements in texture, pigmentation, and scars were common, and adverse effects were generally mild and transient. Melasma relapses occurred, treatment parameters varied considerably, and most studies had moderate-to-high risk of bias. The review supports 1927 nm as promising and clinically useful, but not as a standardized anti-melasma solution ([Oliveira Modena et al., 2025](https://rd.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s10103-025-04781-5.pdf)).

A combination report paired BBL HERO with 1927-nm fractional MOXI, conceptually targeting epidermal pigment with broadband light and superficial dermal pigment with the water-absorbed laser. That approach is discussed below because its clinical evidence is preliminary and difficult to interpret independently of the combination.

### Fractional CO2, Er:YAG, and laser-assisted delivery

Ablative fractional lasers create deeper and more inflammatory microthermal zones than nonablative fractional devices. The potential benefits are stronger remodeling and improved penetration of topical agents. The trade-off is more epidermal disruption, crusting, discomfort, PIH, infection risk, and recovery.

In a prospective split-face trial of 30 patients with refractory melasma, one side received fractional CO2 and the other fractional Q-switched 1064-nm Nd:YAG. All participants also received oral tranexamic acid at 250 mg twice daily, and six sessions were delivered two weeks apart. Patient global assessment favored CO2 at weeks 4, 8, and 12, and MASI declined more on the CO2 side. Erythema and discomfort resolved in less than 24 hours in the report, but the study’s short follow-up and common tranexamic-acid treatment prevent isolation of the laser effect. It supports CO2 as a possible option for carefully selected refractory melasma, not as a first-line universal protocol ([fractional CO2 versus Q-switched Nd:YAG with tranexamic acid](https://doi.org/10.3390/cosmetics8020037)).

A fractional laser can also be used to create microchannels for topical tranexamic acid, vitamin C, cysteamine, or hydroquinone. The rationale is plausible, but the evidence varies by agent, wavelength, dosing, and comparator. Exosome-augmented fractional CO2 treatment is mentioned in recent reviews and small reports, but it remains emerging and lacks large independent comparative trials.

A single case communication illustrates the potential seriousness of pigmentary complications. A Fitzpatrick V patient developed leucoderma after iatrogenic melasma treatment and was treated with fractional Er:YAG and 0.01% bimatoprost. This is not evidence of efficacy or frequency; it is a reminder that treatment-induced hypopigmentation may require specialist management and may be more consequential than the original pigmentation ([Eimpunth et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1097/dss.0000000000003868)).

### Recent laser advances and their clinical maturity

| Advancement | Scientific rationale | Recent evidence | Clinical maturity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fractional 1064-nm picosecond MLA or diffractive optics | Combines photomechanical optical breakdown with fractional dermal remodeling while limiting epidermal injury | In a 30-completer split-face trial, five sessions improved wrinkles, pores, texture, and histologic collagen; results were comparable to fractional Q-switched 1064 nm | Clinically available and reasonably supported for photoaging; superiority over other nonablative fractional systems is unproven |
| 730-nm picosecond treatment | Proposed high melanin selectivity with less vascular collateral absorption; source reports melanin-to-vascular absorption ratio about 3.2:1 versus 1.8:1 for 532 nm | Retrospective mixed-indication study of 131 adults favored 730 nm over 532-nm Q-switched treatment | Promising but emerging; wavelength and pulse duration were confounded, parameter ranges conflicted, and durability was limited |
| 675-nm fractional laser | Intended to combine pigment targeting with dermal remodeling and texture improvement | Recent reviews identify it as promising for melasma and dark skin, but the supplied evidence does not provide a standardized protocol or unified effect estimate | Emerging; insufficient evidence for a universal recommendation |
| Dual 1550/1927-nm systems | Different water-targeted depths permit individualized treatment of texture, photoaging, superficial pigment, and melasma | Fifteen skin-of-color studies show consistent improvement but heterogeneous settings and PIH rates | Established for selected resurfacing and dyschromia applications, especially Fitzpatrick III–IV; less mature for Fitzpatrick VI and long-term melasma |
| Low-fluence 1064-nm plus microsecond 1064-nm delivery | Targets pigment, erythema, superficial vessels, and dermal remodeling | Small split-face trial showed lower relapse at three months but not at six or 12 months | Promising adjunctive protocol, not a proven durable anti-relapse treatment |
| Sequential or combined laser-assisted drug delivery | Addresses pigment, inflammation, and dermal remodeling simultaneously | Small trials and reviews support fractional laser with tranexamic acid or other topical agents; CO2 plus tranexamic acid outperformed QS treatment in one confounded trial | Emerging and operator-dependent |
| Imaging-guided personalization | Uses VISIA, chromametry, melanin meters, RCM, dermoscopy, histology, or optical biopsy to adjust treatment | Objective imaging is increasingly used, but validated algorithms linking imaging to fluence, density, or relapse are not established | Measurement technology is mature; predictive personalization remains investigational |

The direction of progress is therefore clear: shorter pulses, fractional delivery, multiple wavelengths, improved cooling, and image-based monitoring are being combined to widen the therapeutic window. The evidence is not yet strong enough to claim that newer necessarily means better. For several innovations, the strongest supported conclusion is that they are technically plausible and clinically promising, with small or short studies showing feasibility.

## Intense pulsed light: current applications and recent advances

### Spectrum, filtering, and mechanism

IPL systems emit a broad spectrum, commonly described as approximately 500–1200 nm. Cutoff filters remove shorter wavelengths and shape the treatment toward melanin, oxyhemoglobin, or both. The mechanism combines selective absorption by chromophores with controlled bulk heating and, in some protocols, dermal remodeling. IPL can therefore reduce erythema, superficial pigment irregularity, and some textural changes in the same treatment course.

The 2026 Lumenis M22 real-world study used 515–560-nm filters for many vascular and pigmentary indications. Fluence was individualized from 12–18 J/cm² for Fitzpatrick I–III and 10–15 J/cm² for Fitzpatrick IV, with pulse durations of 5–20 ms. The study’s endpoint was mild erythema and transient darkening of pigmented lesions, followed by cooling, moisturization, and sun avoidance ([Fan and Yu, 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12833585/)).

IPL is especially sensitive to treatment context. A filter that is useful for a vascular target may not be appropriate for melasma or darker skin. Broad-spectrum light also exposes melanocytes to wavelengths that may increase pigmentation, particularly when fluence, cooling, pulse structure, or interval is poorly selected.

### IPL modality catalog

| IPL approach | Spectrum and filtering | Main target and outcome | Typical protocol and observed durability | Evidence and safety limits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Conventional facial IPL | Broad emission about 500–1200 nm; cutoff filters commonly 515–560 nm for pigment and vessels | Erythema, superficial dyschromia, mottled pigmentation, pores, fine wrinkles, overall rejuvenation | Recent real-world cohort used at least six sessions; first three at 4–6 weeks, later sessions at 6–8 weeks | Retrospective mixed-indication evidence; response was lower in Fitzpatrick IV and parameters were not fully standardized |
| IPL for solar lentigines | Green or KTP-like filters can concentrate energy toward superficial melanin | Lesion lightening and facial or hand photodamage | Older prospective KTP-filtered IPL evidence reported improvement with minimal downtime but declining effect over six months | Robust lesion-specific 2020–2026 clearance and recurrence data were not retrieved |
| IPL for melasma | Usually 560–1200 nm with cutoff filters, double or triple pulses, 15–30 J/cm², 3–10 ms | Pigment and vascular-inflammatory components | Meta-analysis protocols commonly used four to eight sessions every 2–4 weeks | Stand-alone evidence is inconsistent; a Fitzpatrick IV–V study was negative, while combination QS plus IPL has stronger pooled evidence |
| BBL HERO | Full-spectrum noncoherent light reported as 420–1400 nm; 515 or 560-nm filters, rapid pulses and cooling | Epidermal pigment, vascular change, and photodamage | A nine-patient report used one session followed by 1927-nm MOXI; follow-up ranged from two weeks to 20 months | Preliminary combination evidence; only Fitzpatrick II–III were represented |
| IPL combined with laser or topical therapy | IPL alternated or sequenced with QS laser, fractional laser, tranexamic acid, mesotherapy, or other adjuncts | Multifactorial melasma, pigment plus erythema, or rejuvenation | Protocols vary substantially; QS plus IPL meta-analysis included 31 studies and 2,801 adults | Combination appears more effective than monotherapy for short-term melasma outcomes, but recurrence evidence was low quality |

### Photoaging and multidimensional rejuvenation

A retrospective real-world study of 236 adults treated with six or more Lumenis M22 sessions provides the most substantial recent IPL dataset supplied. The population included 183 Fitzpatrick III and 53 Fitzpatrick IV participants, with acne, rosacea, and cosmetic-rejuvenation groups. In the regular-treatment group, median erythema area decreased from 640.00 to 372.40 mm², hyperpigmentation area from 577.54 to 370.61 mm², and the displayed wrinkle index from 216.60 to 95.00 after the sixth session; all pre/post comparisons were reported as statistically significant.

The study also found that regular treatment was associated with favorable response, with an odds ratio of 13.621, and that total session number was associated with response, odds ratio 3.796. Fitzpatrick IV compared with III predicted lower favorable response, odds ratio 0.121. Transient erythema and edema resolved within 48 hours, and no serious adverse events, scarring, blistering, or prolonged hyperpigmentation were reported.

These findings support IPL as a practical multidimensional rejuvenation tool, but they do not establish causal superiority. The cohort was retrospective, included several diagnoses, lacked a no-treatment or standardized comparator, and allowed clinician-specific filter and fluence adjustments. The source also contains an internal reporting inconsistency: the displayed wrinkle values imply a change from 216.60 to 95.00, whereas the prose reports a median improvement of 123.5. This does not invalidate the direction of the finding, but it limits precise interpretation ([Fan and Yu, 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12833585/)).

The 2026 critical review of IPL literature classified contemporary evidence using Oxford levels and concluded that the strongest recent support lies in erythematotelangiectatic rosacea, meibomian-gland dysfunction, and selected rejuvenation protocols. Melasma, PIH, and broader aesthetic applications remain emerging because studies differ in filters, pulse structures, intervals, concomitant treatments, comparators, and endpoints ([Lee et al., 2026, IPL critical review](https://jcrm.jams.pub/article/1/2/27)).

### Solar lentigines and age spots

IPL is a routine option for solar lentigines because broad light can treat multiple lesions and associated erythema in one session. The supplied evidence, however, does not provide a robust 2020–2026 stand-alone IPL estimate for lesion-specific clearance or long-term recurrence.

A 2019 study summarized in the 2026 532-nm laser review evaluated IPL with a KTP-like filter in 16 Fitzpatrick II–III patients with facial and hand solar lentigines. Significant pigment improvement and minimal downtime were reported, but the effect gradually declined over six months. This is useful context for expected maintenance needs, but it is older, small, and not a direct comparison with a modern picosecond platform ([532-nm green laser review](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9284/13/3/128)).

The BBL HERO plus MOXI report is more recent but does not isolate IPL. Nine patients, all Fitzpatrick II or III, received one combined treatment. BBL HERO used full-face 515- or 560-nm filters, with spot treatments in seven patients, followed by level-3 1927-nm MOXI. The report’s abstract describes a significant VISIA brown-spot improvement, but the displayed full-sample table reports baseline 21.4 versus post-treatment 34.1, mean change 12.7, p=0.11. Only the eight-patient subgroup with reduced pigmentation reached p=0.03. Follow-up varied from two weeks to 20 months, one patient maintained improvement for nearly 20 months, and another followed for approximately 19 months did not improve. No adverse events were reported. This is a hypothesis-generating combination report, not a quantitative estimate of IPL monotherapy clearance ([BBL HERO plus MOXI report](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11460752/)).

### Melasma

Stand-alone IPL for melasma remains controversial. In a prospective study of 32 Fitzpatrick IV–V patients, IPL through 640- and 690-nm filters was delivered monthly for six sessions. Of 26 completers, 12 improved, 10 were unchanged, and 4 deteriorated. MASI changed from 6.70±3.53 to 6.32±3.90, p=0.6891. Erythema and pain were common, and the authors advised against IPL as first-line treatment in darker skin, allowing use only after careful deliberation ([Choudhary et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.2478/sjdv-2020-0001)).

This negative result does not prove that every IPL protocol fails. It does demonstrate that a broad “IPL treats melasma” claim is not transferable across phototypes, filters, fluences, and patient selection. The positive 2026 Fan–Yu cohort did not contain a melasma-specific subgroup, so its generalized reduction in hyperpigmentation cannot override the negative melasma trial.

The strongest recent IPL evidence concerns combination with a Q-switched laser. A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis included 31 controlled studies and 2,801 adults, including 26 randomized and five nonrandomized trials. Compared with monotherapy, QS laser plus IPL produced greater MASI improvement, standardized mean difference −1.20, 95% CI −1.36 to −1.05. The pooled clinical efficacy rate was 92.0% versus 77.4%, with a relative risk of 1.10. Four studies reported recurrence of 8.5% versus 17.8%, relative risk 0.54.

The confidence in these outcomes is not uniform. GRADE rated MASI, clinical efficacy, adverse reactions, and satisfaction as moderate-quality evidence, but recurrence as low-quality because only four studies reported it. The included studies were predominantly East Asian and concentrated in Fitzpatrick III–V. The authors emphasize that at least 12 months of follow-up is needed to establish durability, whereas many studies supplied only short-term data. The pooled result supports a promising combination strategy, not a universal IPL protocol or a definitive long-term anti-recurrence effect ([QS laser plus IPL meta-analysis](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2026.1749950/full)).

## LED and photobiomodulation: current applications and recent advances

### Mechanism and dose

PBM uses low-irradiance red or near-infrared light to modulate cellular activity without deliberate ablation. The best-characterized photoreceptor is mitochondrial cytochrome-c oxidase, which absorbs red light near 665 nm and near-infrared light near 810 nm. Activation is associated with altered ATP production, reactive oxygen species signaling, nitric-oxide modulation, cellular proliferation, and inflammatory regulation. Fibroblasts, keratinocytes, and endothelial cells may all contribute to the clinical response ([Koperdowska, 2026, LED/PBM review](https://journals.viamedica.pl/forum_dermatologicum/article/view/111321)).

PBM has a biphasic dose response. Insufficient energy may not produce a measurable response, while excessive dose can become inhibitory through oxidative stress. The relevant variables are not only total fluence but irradiance, exposure time, wavelength, distance, treatment geometry, and repetition.

The 2026 review reports that consumer masks commonly deliver approximately 5–35 mW/cm² and 1–5 J/cm² per session, although its own summary table gives somewhat different output ranges for red and blue devices. It cites 20–60 J/cm² as a range often considered optimal for full cytochrome-c oxidase activation, but this should not be treated as a universal prescription because biological response depends on wavelength, tissue, and device geometry. Incomplete or inaccurate reporting of PBM parameters is a major barrier to cross-device comparison.

| LED/PBM approach | Wavelength and dose example | Mechanism and target | Clinical findings | Evidence and safety limits |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Red LED | Usually 630–660 nm; one home-mask study used 630±10 nm, 15.6 J/cm², 12 minutes twice weekly | Fibroblast and keratinocyte signaling, ATP and repair pathways, collagen-related remodeling | Fine wrinkles, roughness, dermal density, and tone homogeneity may improve over eight to 12 weeks | Best LED evidence is for modest photoaging improvement; studies are often small and unblinded |
| Amber PBM | About 590 nm; one randomized study used 3.8 J/cm² for 10 sessions over four weeks | Proposed cellular and collagen-related effects, less established than red PBM | Periocular wrinkle volume declined 29.9% in a 137-woman split-face trial; melasma pilot was negative and underpowered | Useful experimental rejuvenation wavelength; not established for melasma |
| Near-infrared PBM | Commonly around 810 nm; dose varies widely | Deeper mitochondrial, nitric-oxide, oxidative-stress, and inflammatory modulation | Mechanistically plausible for repair and inflammation; pigment-specific clinical evidence is sparse | Long-term pigment safety and standardized dosimetry remain uncertain |
| Green LED | 505 nm | Experimental suppression of melanogenesis pathways in cellular and 3D skin models | A human mask intervention reportedly reduced facial pigmentation | Human sample size, schedule, effect size, and durability were unavailable in the supplied report |
| Consumer red-light masks | Device-dependent, often lower output and broad beam geometry | Home PBM with variable tissue dose | AAD summarizes patient-reported improvement in wrinkles, redness, texture, and dark spots | FDA clearance indicates low public risk, not proven effectiveness; darker phototypes may develop more persistent hyperpigmentation |

### Photoaging and rejuvenation

The most informative recent red-LED study enrolled 20 healthy Caucasian volunteers, aged 45–70 years, with signs of facial aging. Participants used a 630±10-nm mask delivering 15.6 J/cm² for 12 minutes twice weekly for three months. At day 84, crow’s-foot depth decreased by 38.3%, dermal density increased by 47.7%, cheek roughness decreased by 23.8%, and complexion homogeneity improved by 34.9%. The measured changes remained at approximately the day-84 level 14 and 28 days after treatment stopped. These results suggest a measurable short-term structural and optical effect, but the study had only 20 participants, no comparator, and allowed usual skincare and makeup throughout. The authors also disclosed relationships with the device company ([Couturaud et al., 2023](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10311288/)).

A larger split-face randomized trial included 137 women aged 40–65 years with Fitzpatrick II–IV skin and Glogau II–IV photoaging. Participants received 10 sessions over four weeks, with 660-nm red PBM on one side and 590-nm amber PBM on the other, both at 3.8 J/cm². Periocular wrinkle volume decreased by 31.6% with red light and 29.9% with amber light. Neither treatment improved hydration or viscoelasticity, although quality-of-life questionnaires improved. This is stronger comparative evidence for wrinkle volume than for dermal remodeling, and it does not establish long-term maintenance ([red and amber PBM trial](https://sage.cnpereading.com/doi/10.1089/photob.2022.0114)).

The 2026 PBM review also summarizes a study of 31 participants who received nine LED sessions. Reported improvements included periorbital wrinkles, elasticity, smoothness, and firmness, with more than half of participants rating improvement at 25–50%. The treatment was well tolerated, but direct collagen measurement and long-term follow-up were not reported in the review summary ([Koperdowska, 2026](https://journals.viamedica.pl/forum_dermatologicum/article/view/111321)).

The American Academy of Dermatology summarizes one facial red-light study in which 90 patients received eight treatments over four weeks; more than 90% reported some improvement, including softer and smoother skin, less redness, and lightening of dark spots. The AAD cautions that differing devices, treatment durations, and study designs prevent direct comparison and that more research is needed to determine optimal dosing and maintenance ([AAD red-light guidance](https://www.aad.org/public/cosmetic/safety/red-light-therapy)).

### Brightening and pigmentary outcomes

LED studies reporting “complexion homogeneity,” “luminosity,” “dark-spot lightening,” or melanin-index changes do not establish generalized whitening. A more even complexion may reflect reduced erythema, reduced focal pigmentation, improved optical uniformity, or altered hydration and surface reflection.

The 505-nm green-LED work is a notable recent development but remains preliminary. In B16 mouse melanoma cells and three-dimensional skin models, 505-nm light reduced microphthalmia-associated transcription factor and tyrosinase expression and reduced melanin without affecting cell viability. A human facial-mask intervention also reportedly decreased pigmentation. However, the supplied human report gives no sample size, treatment schedule, numerical effect size, or durability. The appropriate classification is mechanistic and early clinical evidence, not an established depigmentation treatment ([Mima et al., 2025/2026 version](https://doi.org/10.2340/actadv.v105.43441)).

### Melasma and darker skin

No high-quality randomized clinical evidence establishes LED or PBM as an effective treatment for melasma. A 2025 double-blind randomized pilot trial compared active amber PBM with placebo cream against sham PBM with 5% liposomal tranexamic-acid cream for 12 weeks. Only 21 women were randomized, 10 to PBM and 11 to tranexamic acid. MASI and physician global assessment did not differ significantly within or between groups. The study ended early with only 51% statistical power, so it cannot exclude a modest effect, but it cannot establish efficacy. PBM caused warmth; tranexamic acid caused burning, and transient increased pigmentation occurred in the tranexamic-acid group at week six ([Galache et al., 2025](https://www.springermedicine.com/tranexamic-acid/melasma/amber-led-photobiomodulation-versus-tranexamic-acid-for-the-trea/51214274)).

The pigmentary risk of visible light is clinically important. The 2026 PBM review reports that 400–700-nm exposure produced darker and more persistent pigmentation in Fitzpatrick IV–VI than UVA1, with pigment persisting up to 14 days and a dose response. The effect was absent in phototype II. On that basis, the review advises caution or avoidance of visible-light LED therapy in melasma, particularly in darker phototypes, and recommends visible-light-inclusive photoprotection.

This creates an important disagreement between marketing-oriented claims and clinical caution. The 2023 red-mask study states that its design allowed inclusion of phototypes V and VI without risk, but the cohort and design were not adequate to establish long-term pigment safety in those groups. The AAD likewise warns that darker skin tones are more sensitive to visible red light and may develop more intense and longer-lasting hyperpigmentation. Red light may be safe for many users in the short term, but “non-UV” does not mean “pigment-neutral” for every patient.

### LED safety and practical role

Short-term adverse effects are generally mild: warmth, transient pain, irritation, dryness, or erythema. LED devices do not normally produce the crusting, blistering, or prolonged wound care associated with ablative resurfacing. Their low downtime is a major practical advantage.

Safety is nevertheless dependent on wavelength, output, eye protection, photosensitivity, and the treated person’s pigment biology. The AAD recommends dermatologist review for people with photosensitive conditions such as lupus, those taking photosensitizing medication, and those who need device-specific eye protection. It also emphasizes that FDA clearance means the device is considered low risk, not that its effectiveness has been proven.

For aesthetic medicine, the most defensible role of LED/PBM is adjunctive or maintenance-oriented treatment for mild photoaging, barrier recovery, and selected inflammatory or reparative goals. It should not replace diagnosis and treatment of melasma or focal pigmented lesions, and it should not be marketed as a validated generalized whitening method.

## Photoaging and skin brightening outcomes

### What improves most reliably

Across modalities, the best-supported photoaging outcomes are reduction in fine wrinkles, roughness, pores, mottled pigmentation, and visible erythema. The relative strength of each modality depends on whether the primary target is texture, focal pigment, diffuse dyschromia, or vascular change.

A 2025 split-face trial comparing fractional 1064-nm picosecond Nd:YAG with fractional Q-switched 1064-nm Nd:YAG illustrates the importance of separating within-treatment improvement from between-device superiority. Thirty participants with Fitzpatrick III–IV skin received five sessions at weeks 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8. At three months after the final session, wrinkle counts fell from 84.53±25.75 to 52.17±26.11 on the picosecond side and from 89.43±25.22 to 50.23±22.18 on the Q-switched side. Pores, texture, and histologic collagen and elastic-fiber organization also improved. None of the between-modality differences in wrinkles, pores, texture, semi-quantitative score, or GAIS was statistically significant. The trial supports comparable photoaging efficacy, not a proven picosecond advantage ([Tang et al., 2025](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12210001/)).

Histology showed increased collagen and improved elastic-fiber alignment on both sides. More pronounced collagen proliferation on the picosecond side was described, but only three participants underwent biopsy and the difference was not statistically significant. Histologic remodeling is therefore a plausible mechanism, not a validated reason to promise superior clinical collagen stimulation.

A 2026 double-blind split-face trial of one 1064-nm picosecond session followed by eight weeks of a multifunctional serum provides a different kind of evidence. Twenty-four women aged 30–48 years received the same laser on both sides, followed by serum on one side and placebo on the other. At day 57, the serum side had a 25.0% higher efficacy rate for overall photoaging assessment and a 20.83% higher efficacy rate for fine wrinkles. Melanin index fell 10.45% from baseline on the serum side versus 5.13% on the placebo side. The result supports an aftercare effect in a small, short trial; it does not isolate the laser’s independent contribution or support generalized whitening ([He et al., 2026](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13144715/)).

### Objective versus subjective improvement

Objective tools increasingly shape aesthetic studies, but they measure different constructs:

- VISIA quantifies image-derived erythema, pigmentation, pores, or wrinkles using proprietary indices.
- Chromametry measures color coordinates or differences between facial sites.
- Melanin meters estimate optical melanin content.
- PRIMOS or similar systems measure wrinkle volume or area.
- Cutometry measures deformation and elastic recovery.
- Ultrasound estimates dermal density.
- Reflectance confocal microscopy visualizes cellular and structural patterns.
- Histology can demonstrate collagen, elastin, melanocyte, or melanin changes in biopsied skin.

These endpoints cannot be assumed interchangeable. A lower VISIA pigment index may represent fewer visible spots, reduced contrast, or altered image characteristics; it is not automatically equivalent to a percentage reduction in melanin. A patient’s satisfaction may improve without a large MASI change, or an objective index may improve without a corresponding perceived benefit.

The QS-plus-IPL meta-analysis demonstrates this distinction. Objective MASI and clinical efficacy favored combination treatment, but patient satisfaction did not differ significantly. The authors attribute this possible divergence to expectations, fear of relapse, transient treatment effects, and the limited sensitivity of simple satisfaction scales. A high-quality clinical assessment should therefore include both standardized objective measures and validated patient-reported outcomes.

### Collagen and tissue remodeling

The mechanistic rationale for collagen remodeling is strongest for fractional thermal injury and red/NIR PBM. Fractional 1550- and 1927-nm studies report increased collagen, elastic fibers, and hyaluronic acid. Fractional 1064-nm picosecond and Q-switched studies show histologic collagen and elastin organization. Red and amber PBM studies report wrinkle-volume reduction, while the biological rationale invokes fibroblast activation and mitochondrial signaling.

Direct clinical evidence of collagen quantity remains sparse. Many studies infer remodeling from histology, ultrasound density, wrinkle reduction, or texture changes. These measures should be reported separately. A visible improvement in wrinkle volume is clinically meaningful even if direct collagen quantification is unavailable, but it should not be described as proof that a specific device produces a defined amount of new collagen.

### Timing and durability

Treatment speed is highly protocol-dependent:

- A pigment-selective 532-nm laser may visibly alter a discrete lentigo after one session, but short-term clearance does not establish permanence.
- Fractional photoaging treatment typically requires a series of sessions, with improvement developing over weeks as epidermal renewal and dermal remodeling occur.
- IPL commonly requires repeated treatments; the 2026 real-world cohort associated regular intervals and more sessions with better outcomes.
- LED/PBM generally requires repeated home or clinic sessions over four to 12 weeks and maintenance treatments.
- Melasma improvement may appear within one to three months but often declines after treatment stops.

The best supplied durability data are heterogeneous. The red LED mask study observed persistence at 14 and 28 days after stopping. The combined long-pulse 1064 plus picosecond 755-nm trial reported GAIS benefits at three and six months. The 1064-nm melasma trial followed participants to week 24, but all used intensive sunscreen. The dual-mode melasma trial followed patients for 12 months and showed that an early relapse difference disappeared by six and 12 months. These results support maintenance rather than a one-time cure model.

### Brightening is not generalized whitening

The available clinical literature supports four narrower claims:

1. Visible dark spots or mottled pigmentation may decrease.
2. Uneven facial tone may become more uniform.
3. Erythema may decline, making the complexion appear brighter.
4. Melanin-index or chromametric values may improve in treated areas.

It does not support a claim that lasers, IPL, or LED safely and predictably lighten a person’s overall natural skin color. The distinction is clinically important because generalized whitening language can encourage excessive treatment, obscure PIH or hypopigmentation, and reinforce ethically problematic color hierarchies. Aesthetic documentation should identify the lesion or endpoint being treated and should state whether the outcome is objective, subjective, calculated, or hypothetical.

## Hyperpigmentation: solar lentigines versus melasma

The two conditions should not be combined into one “pigmentation” category. Their biology, treatment goals, risk-benefit balance, and durability are different.

| Feature | Solar lentigines or age spots | Melasma | Clinical consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Typical appearance | Discrete, sharply demarcated macules on sun-exposed skin | Symmetric patches, commonly on the cheeks, forehead, upper lip, or jaw | Lesion-selective treatment is more straightforward for lentigines |
| Dominant biology | Epidermal melanin, altered dermal-epidermal junction, chronic photoexposure | Melanocyte hyperactivity plus vascular, inflammatory, hormonal, dermal, and basement-membrane changes | Melasma requires multi-target management |
| Treatment objective | Clearance or substantial lightening of defined lesions | Reduction of disease activity and maintenance of natural tone | Complete clearance is less realistic for melasma |
| Typical procedural response | Often rapid after one or a few sessions | Gradual improvement after repeated treatment; relapse common | Maintenance and photoprotection are central in melasma |
| Main procedural risk | PIH, hypopigmentation, incomplete clearance, misdiagnosis | PIH, mottled hypopigmentation, rebound pigmentation, recurrence | Aggressive treatment can worsen melasma |
| Diagnostic priority | Dermoscopy and biopsy when uncertain | Confirm diagnosis and depth with clinical examination, Wood’s lamp, dermoscopy, or biopsy when necessary | Neither condition should be treated solely from a marketing label |

### Solar lentigines and age spots

#### Efficacy and speed

For a clearly diagnosed superficial lentigo, pigment-selective lasers provide the most direct mechanism. The 532-nm picosecond versus Q-switched trial found better blinded improvement at 12 weeks with picosecond delivery, with a possible reduction in PIH. A 2026 five-lesion millisecond green-laser case series reported 5/5 complete responses at day 21. These findings support rapid lesion lightening, but they should not be converted into a universal “clearance rate.” The five-lesion series had no comparator and only 21 days of follow-up.

The 730-nm retrospective study reported higher improvement across mixed pigmentation disorders, but it did not provide a robust solar-lentigine-specific clearance result. Its 60 solar-lentigine participants were pooled with 42 melasma and 29 PIH participants. Because diagnosis, wavelength, pulse duration, fluence, and treatment number differed, the result is a broad facial-pigmentation signal rather than a definitive age-spot comparison.

IPL can be useful when lentigines coexist with diffuse photodamage or erythema, but the supplied 2020–2026 evidence does not establish a robust modern IPL monotherapy clearance rate for solar lentigines. A KTP-filtered IPL study summarized in the 2026 review found improvement with minimal downtime, followed by gradual decline over six months. This suggests that IPL may be appropriate for broad photorejuvenation and multiple superficial lesions, while a narrowly targeted laser may be preferable when the main goal is rapid clearance of a small number of sharply defined spots.

#### Durability and recurrence

Short-term disappearance is not the same as durable clearance. Solar lentigines arise in chronically photoexposed skin, and structural changes in the dermal-epidermal junction may persist after visible pigment is reduced. The 532-nm green-laser case series explicitly states that its 21-day follow-up could not assess recurrence, delayed PIH, durability, or later adverse effects. The BBL-MOXI report included a patient with nearly 20 months of maintained improvement, but follow-up was variable, one patient had no improvement at approximately 19 months, and sunscreen adherence was unknown.

Long-term recurrence estimates for solar lentigines remain unavailable or inconsistent in the supplied evidence. New lesions can arise from continued sun exposure even when the treated lesion remains clear. Maintenance therefore consists less of repeated automatic laser treatment than of photoprotection, diagnostic monitoring, and treatment of clinically significant recurrence.

#### PIH and hypopigmentation

The main risk in darker skin is not simply incomplete clearance but a new, more noticeable pigmentary abnormality. In the 532-nm split-face trial, PIH was 5% after picosecond treatment and 30% after Q-switched treatment, although the comparison was not statistically significant. The 2026 532-nm review emphasizes that device type, pulse structure, fluence, endpoint, and phototype all affect PIH.

Picosecond treatment may reduce heat diffusion, but it does not eliminate PIH. Conservative endpoints, limited overlap, adequate cooling, and careful aftercare remain important. Hypopigmentation is less frequently reported in the lentigine studies but can occur after pigment-selective treatment, especially with repeated or excessive energy. Confetti-like or guttate depigmentation is a recognized concern in low-fluence and repeated laser practice, although standardized frequency estimates were not available in the supplied evidence.

#### Diagnostic safety

A pigmented macule that is treated cosmetically without adequate assessment may become difficult to monitor or may delay diagnosis of melanoma. The 2026 green-laser report excluded lesions with dermoscopic features suggestive of pigmented actinic keratosis, lichen planus-like keratosis, seborrheic keratosis, or lentigo maligna. Specialist evaluation and biopsy should be considered for asymmetric, changing, multicolored, atypical, symptomatic, or diagnostically uncertain lesions.

### Melasma

#### Why melasma is more difficult

Melasma is not only an excess of epidermal melanin. The condition may include dermal melanophages, vascular dilation, mast-cell activity, solar elastosis, fibroblast senescence, basement-membrane disruption, and hormonal or inflammatory drivers. A procedure that removes visible pigment without addressing triggers can produce an impressive early result followed by relapse.

The AAD states that there is no single best treatment and that management usually combines sunscreen, medication, and sometimes a procedure. It describes laser and light treatments as options that a dermatologist may add when patients are already using medication and sun protection, not as an established stand-alone whitening protocol ([AAD melasma guidance](https://www.aad.org/public/diseases/a-z/melasma-treatment)).

#### Picosecond and Q-switched lasers

The 2023 randomized trial supports 1064-nm picosecond Nd:YAG as a useful option for selected Fitzpatrick III–IV patients. Its 35.9% MASI improvement at week 24 was greater than that of 755-nm picosecond treatment and 2% hydroquinone. The result may reflect both wavelength and pulse duration: 1064 nm penetrates more deeply and is less absorbed by epidermal melanin than 755 nm, while 450 ps may produce a more photomechanical effect than the 750-ps 755-nm protocol. The trial was not designed to isolate those variables.

Other head-to-head comparisons do not show a universal picosecond advantage. A 2022 prospective split-face study summarized in the laser review found comparable modified MASI and melanin-index results between picosecond and conventional 1064-nm Nd:YAG. Thus, picosecond superiority is indication-dependent and cannot be generalized from solar lentigines to melasma.

Low-fluence 1064-nm treatment remains clinically common, but repeated treatment carries risks of mottled hypopigmentation, rebound pigmentation, and diminishing benefit. The dual-mode LFQS plus microsecond trial illustrates that adding a vascular and remodeling target may improve early relapse metrics, but the difference was gone at 12 months.

#### Fractional 1550- and 1927-nm lasers

Fractional nonablative treatment may be useful when melasma coexists with texture change or when a clinician wishes to target pigment and photoaging with less epidermal injury than ablative resurfacing. In the skin-of-color review, 1550-nm studies reported approximately 18% MASI improvement in one study, while 1927-nm studies reported 10–33% improvements in small Asian cohorts. PIH occurred in approximately 9–18% of participants across several melasma studies, and prolonged erythema was more likely with higher energy.

The 1927-nm laser’s water targeting may offer a wider therapeutic window than lower-wavelength pigment lasers, but the advantage is relative, not absolute. The review of 17 studies and 448 participants found parameter variability and moderate-to-high risk of bias, with relapses in melasma. The best-supported use is selected, phototype-adjusted treatment with careful aftercare, not unsupervised or high-density resurfacing.

#### Fractional CO2 and combination therapy

Fractional CO2 may be considered in refractory cases with substantial textural or dermal components, especially when topical delivery is part of the treatment rationale. The 30-person split-face trial favored CO2 over fractional QS Nd:YAG, but all participants received oral tranexamic acid. The laser effect therefore cannot be separated from the drug, and the short follow-up cannot establish durable superiority.

Recent reviews also describe fractional laser-assisted delivery of tranexamic acid, vitamin C, cysteamine, and other agents. These protocols are biologically plausible and may be useful in specialist practice, but they remain heterogeneous in laser settings, drug concentration, application timing, and maintenance regimen.

#### IPL and QS-plus-IPL combinations

The negative 2020 IPL study in Fitzpatrick IV–V should be treated as important counterevidence, especially against first-line IPL monotherapy in darker skin. The later 2026 meta-analysis supports QS laser plus IPL over either modality alone for short-term MASI and clinical efficacy. The difference may reflect the complementary targets: QS laser disrupts melanin, while IPL may influence melanin, superficial hemoglobin, vascular inflammation, extracellular matrix, and basement-membrane changes.

That mechanistic explanation remains partly inferential. The meta-analysis included 31 studies with heterogeneous devices, schedules, and outcome definitions; parameter-level pooling was not possible. Combination treatment may also benefit from additional clinical contact, more total sessions, or selection of patients likely to respond. The evidence supports considering combination therapy in selected melasma, not treating the pooled rate of 92.0% as an individual probability of cure.

#### Sun and visible-light protection

Photoprotection is not an optional afterthought. UV exposure, visible light, and heat can reactivate melanogenesis. Broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher is commonly recommended, with iron oxide-containing tinted formulations particularly relevant for visible-light protection. The 2026 photoprotection review summarized a 39-person Fitzpatrick III–V comparative study in which tinted iron-oxide sunscreen reduced melasma relapse more than a colorless formula. Tinted makeup over a colorless sunscreen did not produce the same additional protection, suggesting that spectral coverage rather than color alone matters.

For patients undergoing laser or IPL, the relevant prescription is behavioral as well as topical: avoid intentional tanning, use shade and physical protection, apply sunscreen adequately and repeatedly, and defer treatment when the skin is recently tanned, inflamed, or irritated. Without these measures, a favorable short-term procedural result may simply reflect temporary suppression of pigment under controlled conditions.

#### Topical and systemic adjuncts

Topical hydroquinone, retinoids, corticosteroid-containing triple combinations, azelaic acid, kojic acid, vitamin C, niacinamide, cysteamine, and tranexamic acid occupy different positions depending on jurisdiction, patient risk, and tolerance. Oral tranexamic acid can be effective for selected patients but requires medical assessment of thromboembolic risk. AAD guidance emphasizes that patients with a history of blood clots should disclose this before oral tranexamic acid is prescribed.

The laser and light literature often includes adjunctive sunscreen, hydroquinone, tranexamic acid, or standard skincare. When an intervention study includes these agents in every arm, the study estimates the combined regimen rather than the device alone. This distinction should be preserved in clinical counseling and scientific reporting.

## Cross-modality comparison, combination treatment, and personalization

### Comparison on shared clinical axes

No direct standardized trial permits a universal ranking of laser, IPL, and LED. The table below therefore combines direct comparisons within each modality with the strongest supported cross-study judgment.

| Shared axis | Laser | IPL | LED/PBM | Supported judgment |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Photoaging efficacy | Strongest for texture, wrinkles, pores, and remodeling when fractional or picosecond systems are used; ablative systems are more aggressive | Useful for combined erythema, mottled pigment, and mild textural change; repeated sessions usually required | Modest improvement in fine wrinkles, roughness, and perceived skin quality | Lasers generally offer greater procedural effect; IPL is broader; LED is gentler and slower |
| Solar lentigines | Most direct and rapid option for defined superficial lesions, especially 532-nm pigment-selective systems | Useful for multiple lesions and diffuse photodamage, but modern lesion-specific clearance data are limited | Not established for lesion clearance; dark-spot improvement is mostly patient-reported or nonspecific | Laser has the clearest focal-lesion role |
| Melasma | Can improve selected cases, especially low-fluence 1064-nm and carefully chosen fractional protocols, but relapse and PIH remain concerns | Monotherapy evidence is inconsistent; QS plus IPL has better pooled short-term outcomes | No high-quality evidence of efficacy; visible light may worsen pigment in darker phototypes | All procedural options are adjunctive; LED is not currently a treatment for melasma |
| Speed and sessions | Focal laser may work in one session; fractional and melasma protocols usually require three to ten sessions | Commonly four to eight sessions for melasma and six or more for maintenance-style rejuvenation | Usually repeated twice weekly or in multi-session courses over four to 12 weeks | Speed depends more on indication and protocol than device label |
| Durability | Focal clearance may be durable but recurrence data are sparse; melasma commonly relapses | Rejuvenation and pigment benefits may decline without maintenance; recurrence evidence is limited | Short-term persistence has been reported, but maintenance is usually needed | None provides reliable permanent control of melasma |
| Downtime and tolerability | Nonablative systems usually produce transient erythema, edema, dryness, or petechiae; ablative CO2 has greater recovery | Usually short erythema or edema, but burns and PIH are possible | Usually no downtime; warmth or irritation can occur | LED is best tolerated, but lower intensity does not guarantee pigment safety |
| Suitability by phototype | Wavelength, energy, density, cooling, and diagnosis must be adjusted; 1550/1927 may widen the window for skin of color | Conservative fluence and longer intervals are important; response may be lower in Fitzpatrick IV | Darker skin may be more sensitive to visible red light and develop longer-lasting hyperpigmentation | No modality is intrinsically safe independent of dose and phototype |
| Evidence certainty | Moderate for selected laser-indication pairs; emerging for 730, 675, and some combinations | Moderate for QS-plus-IPL MASI outcomes; heterogeneous for monotherapy and lentigines | Moderate or promising for photoaging but low for pigment disorders | Evidence must be rated by indication, not by technology category |

### Combination and sequential treatment

#### Q-switched laser plus IPL

The 2026 meta-analysis provides the strongest quantitative support for a light-based combination. MASI, clinical efficacy, and adverse-reaction outcomes were rated moderate quality; recurrence was low quality. The combination’s rationale is multi-target treatment of pigment, superficial vascular change, inflammation, and photoaging-related dermal alterations.

The limitation is that the combination literature is largely regional and heterogeneous. Most studies were conducted in China or East Asia and concentrated in Fitzpatrick III–V. Treatment frequency, order, filter, fluence, and number of sessions differed. A clinician should therefore use the meta-analysis as support for a treatment strategy, not as a validated dosing algorithm.

#### BBL HERO plus 1927-nm MOXI

The BBL-MOXI report illustrates a plausible depth-based sequence: BBL targets epidermal melanin through 515- or 560-nm filters, then 1927 nm addresses water-rich superficial dermal tissue. One session produced marked photographic improvements in several patients, but the full nine-person VISIA analysis was not statistically significant, and only Fitzpatrick II–III were represented.

The sequence is therefore clinically interesting but immature. It should not be described as proven safe for all skin types merely because the device is marketed broadly; the actual evidence supplied contains no direct outcome data for Fitzpatrick IV–VI.

#### LFQS plus microsecond 1064 nm

The dual-mode protocol is notable because it targets pigment and erythema or vascular inflammation in the same wavelength family. The early reduction in relapse at three months was not sustained at six or 12 months. The result supports biologic plausibility and short-term clinical benefit, but not a definitive anti-recurrence effect.

#### Laser plus topical agents

The most mature combination concept is procedural treatment plus photoprotection and topical pigment control. Fractional lasers can improve topical penetration, while hydroquinone, tranexamic acid, retinoids, niacinamide, or cysteamine can address ongoing melanogenesis and inflammation. The exact contribution of the laser varies by trial. The 1927-nm hyperpigmentation study found approximately 50% index improvement with or without hydroquinone, while hydroquinone improved investigator-rated GAIS at week 12. This demonstrates why index reduction, global assessment, and satisfaction should all be reported.

#### Multi-laser photoaging protocols

A 2025 two-center randomized split-face trial treated the full face with long-pulse 1064-nm Nd:YAG and one side with additional picosecond 755-nm alexandrite using a diffractive lens array. Three sessions were delivered at monthly intervals in 22 volunteers, with 21 completing. At three months, GAIS improvement was 85.7% on the combined side versus 66.7% with 1064 nm alone; at six months, the corresponding values were 66.7% and 57.1%. VISIA showed pigmentation and pore improvement at one and three months, and no adverse events were observed. The authors characterized the findings as preliminary, and the small two-center sample does not establish an optimized sequence ([Wu et al., 2025](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41405728/)).

### Imaging, measurement, and personalization

VISIA, chromametry, melanin meters, dermoscopy, RCM, histology, ultrasound, and 3D wrinkle analysis have improved measurement quality. Their current roles are primarily descriptive and monitoring-based:

- Dermoscopy and Wood’s lamp help distinguish lesion type and pigment depth before treatment.
- VISIA and ImageJ can quantify relative erythema and pigment area.
- Chromametry can quantify tone homogeneity and lightness differences.
- Melanin meters can track optical melanin changes over time.
- RCM and histology can show epidermal, dermal, collagen, elastic-fiber, or melanocyte changes.
- Repeated standardized imaging can reveal relapse that a single subjective photograph may miss.

These tools are not yet interchangeable or universally validated. VISIA’s proprietary wrinkle or pigment indices may not be directly comparable across devices or studies. Confocal microscopy and histology are valuable for mechanism but are not practical routine endpoints for every patient.

The research direction is toward image-guided personalization. A recent melasma review discusses AI-assisted assessment, optical biopsy, and biomarker-based stratification, but validated systems that prescribe wavelength, fluence, density, cooling, or session number were not demonstrated in the supplied evidence. Personalization remains a clinical judgment informed by phototype, pigment depth, prior response, and early treatment reaction rather than an established algorithm.

### What can reasonably be ranked

A conditional ranking is more defensible than a universal one:

- For a small number of well-diagnosed solar lentigines, pigment-selective laser treatment has the strongest direct evidence for rapid focal clearance.
- For broad photoaging with erythema, mottled pigment, and mild textural change, IPL offers useful multi-target treatment and may be more efficient than treating separate features independently.
- For wrinkles and texture where downtime is acceptable, fractional laser treatment has a stronger remodeling rationale than LED, with the choice between nonablative and ablative systems determined by severity and phototype.
- For melasma, no modality reliably eliminates relapse. Low-fluence 1064-nm approaches, selected fractional lasers, and QS-plus-IPL combinations can be considered within a broader management plan.
- For mild photoaging when minimal downtime is essential, LED/PBM is a reasonable adjunct or maintenance option, but its effects are generally subtler and slower.
- For generalized whitening, none of the modalities has an evidence-based indication.

## Safety, limitations, and research gaps

### Adverse effects by modality

Laser-related adverse effects depend on wavelength, pulse duration, fluence, density, spot size, overlap, cooling, aftercare, and skin phototype.

Pigment-selective 532-, 730-, 755-, and 1064-nm lasers can cause pain, transient erythema, edema, purpura, crusting, PIH, hypopigmentation, and, rarely, scarring. The shorter pulse of a picosecond system may reduce heat diffusion but does not remove the risk of inflammation. Repeated low-fluence treatment can produce uneven hypopigmentation or paradoxical pigment change.

Nonablative fractional 1550- and 1927-nm lasers commonly produce erythema, edema, dryness, roughness, petechiae, mild itching, or transient pigment alteration. PIH becomes more likely with higher fluence, higher density, greater coverage, and darker phototype. The 1550/1927 review consistently associates lower energy and density with fewer PIH events.

Ablative fractional CO2 and Er:YAG lasers add crusting, scaling, wound-care needs, infection risk, prolonged erythema, and potentially greater PIH or scarring. Their capacity to improve texture or facilitate topical delivery may justify the risk in selected patients, but their use for melasma should be conservative.

IPL can cause pain, erythema, edema, blistering, crusting, PIH, or hypopigmentation. The 2026 real-world cohort reported only transient erythema and edema resolving within 48 hours, but its patients were mainly Fitzpatrick III–IV and its settings were individualized. A favorable retrospective safety profile should not be generalized to recently tanned skin, high fluence, darker phototypes, or different devices.

LED/PBM usually causes mild warmth, irritation, dryness, or transient pain. The clinically important exception is pigment darkening from visible light, especially in Fitzpatrick IV–VI or people with melasma. Long-term effects of consumer devices remain incompletely characterized.

### Contraindications and specialist precautions

A complete device- and wavelength-specific contraindication matrix was not supplied and cannot be inferred. The following are evidence-supported precautions rather than an exhaustive universal list:

- Evaluate photosensitivity, lupus, active dermatitis, infection, open wounds, and recent sun exposure before treatment.
- Review photosensitizing medications and treatments.
- Defer treatment on recently tanned or inflamed skin.
- Consider pregnancy and lactation exclusions according to the device, indication, and local clinical guidance; the relevant trials commonly excluded these groups.
- Assess history of keloid or hypertrophic scarring, especially before ablative or high-density fractional treatment.
- Review prior PIH, hypopigmentation, or poor response to energy-based treatment.
- Consider antiviral prophylaxis for patients with recurrent facial HSV. In the 2025 fractional photoaging trial, two participants with recurrent HSV experienced reactivation and recovered with antiviral treatment.
- Use wavelength-specific eye protection and follow device instructions.
- Use test spots or conservative initial settings when phototype, diagnosis, or prior response creates uncertainty.
- Avoid cosmetic treatment of lesions that are changing, asymmetric, atypical, symptomatic, or diagnostically uncertain until specialist evaluation is complete.

The AAD advises dermatologist assessment before home red-light use, particularly for darker skin tones, photosensitive diseases, photosensitizing medications, and eye-protection requirements ([AAD red-light guidance](https://www.aad.org/public/cosmetic/safety/red-light-therapy)).

### Paradoxical pigmentation and hypopigmentation

Paradoxical darkening can result from treatment-induced inflammation, visible-light exposure, excessive thermal injury, inadequate photoprotection, hormonal or environmental triggers, or recurrence of the underlying disease. It is particularly relevant in melasma because the condition is already inflammation-sensitive.

Hypopigmentation may occur through melanocyte injury, repeated subthreshold treatment, or excessive cumulative energy. The 2023 case of leucoderma after iatrogenic melasma treatment demonstrates that pigmentary injury can be persistent and psychologically significant. The possibility of hypopigmentation should be discussed before repeated laser toning or aggressive pigment treatment.

The clinical target should be a favorable net pigment balance: less visible disease with no unacceptable new dyspigmentation. A study that reports only the percentage of lesions cleared but not PIH, hypopigmentation, or recurrence is incomplete for darker skin.

### Long-term follow-up and endpoint problems

Long-term follow-up is the central limitation of the literature:

- Many solar-lentigine reports end at four to 12 weeks.
- Many photoaging studies end at three to six months.
- Melasma trials often report three to 12 months, but only a minority provide robust relapse definitions.
- LED studies commonly measure results immediately after a treatment course or within one month of stopping.
- Newer wavelengths such as 730, 675, and 1927 nm lack large independent studies with multi-year follow-up.

The 2026 QS-plus-IP​​L meta-analysis required at least three months of follow-up, but its authors still state that at least 12 months is needed to establish melasma durability. The dual-mode 1064-nm trial, which did follow patients for 12 months, found that an early relapse difference disappeared by the end of follow-up. This illustrates why short-term response rates should not be described as anti-recurrence effects.

Endpoint standardization is another problem. MASI, modified MASI, physician global assessment, GAIS, quartile scales, VISIA indices, colorimetry, melanin index, and patient satisfaction measure overlapping but nonidentical outcomes. Clinical efficacy rates in the QS-plus-IPL literature were sometimes defined as more than 30% MASI improvement or more than 30% lesion-area reduction plus visible lightening. These definitions may not transfer across countries or clinical systems.

### Evidence design and causal attribution

Many recent studies are small, retrospective, uncontrolled, or single-center:

- The 532-nm green-laser report included five lesions.
- The BBL-MOXI report included nine patients.
- The 730-nm comparison was retrospective and confounded by wavelength and pulse duration.
- The red LED mask study included 20 participants without a comparator.
- The amber melasma PBM trial included 21 participants and ended early.
- The 2025 photoaging combination laser study included 21 completers.
- The 2026 1064-nm serum trial included 24 women and tested serum after identical laser treatment on both sides.

These studies can identify feasibility, signals of benefit, and technical issues. They cannot establish universal efficacy, optimal dosing, or long-term safety.

Even randomized trials may not isolate the device effect if all groups receive sunscreen, tranexamic acid, hydroquinone, or standardized skincare. This is not a flaw when the clinical question is whether a complete regimen works, but it must be reported honestly. The result estimates the regimen, not the energy device alone.

### Regulatory and ethical context

Regulatory clearance and clinical effectiveness are separate concepts. The AAD explains that “FDA-cleared” indicates a device is considered low risk to the public; it does not establish that the device is effective for every marketed claim. “FDA approved” or “FDA certified” are not interchangeable terms for devices.

Cross-jurisdictional regulatory status for the many laser, IPL, BBL, MOXI, and consumer LED systems is not uniform in the supplied evidence. A device’s indication, wavelength, handpiece, and software may vary across regions. Clinicians should therefore verify the local regulatory indication and avoid equating clearance with a high-certainty clinical recommendation.

The language of skin whitening requires additional ethical care. A treatment that restores natural tone after melasma or removes a sun-induced spot is clinically distinct from treating healthy skin to conform to an external color ideal. Reporting should identify the treated lesion, use objective or validated patient-centered endpoints, and disclose any hypopigmentation or color mismatch. Marketing claims that imply safe, uniform, permanent lightening of overall skin color are not supported by the evidence reviewed here.

### Situations requiring specialist evaluation

Specialist assessment is particularly important when:

- a pigmented lesion is new, changing, asymmetric, multicolored, bleeding, or diagnostically uncertain;
- melasma is severe, recurrent, dermal, or associated with hormonal medication or pregnancy;
- the patient has Fitzpatrick V–VI skin and seeks high-energy pigment treatment;
- there is a history of PIH, hypopigmentation, keloid formation, HSV, photosensitivity, or autoimmune disease;
- the patient is taking photosensitizing medication, anticoagulants, or considering oral tranexamic acid;
- pigmentation followed a prior cosmetic procedure and may represent iatrogenic injury;
- the proposed treatment is ablative, high-density, or a multi-device sequence;
- a consumer LED device is being considered for melasma or darker skin.

## Closing judgment

Laser, IPL, and LED are not three interchangeable versions of the same treatment. Lasers offer the greatest control over pigment depth, pulse duration, and fractional remodeling; IPL offers broad, multi-target treatment of vascular, pigmentary, and mild textural changes; LED/PBM offers low-downtime, lower-intensity modulation with the clearest evidence for modest photoaging improvement.

For solar lentigines, pigment-selective laser treatment has the strongest direct short-term evidence, although recurrence and long-term safety are underreported. For photoaging, fractional lasers and IPL provide more substantial procedural remodeling, while red or amber PBM can offer a gentler adjunctive effect. For melasma, every light-based modality must be framed as part of chronic management: photoprotection and topical or systemic therapy remain foundational, and short-term pigment reduction should never be confused with durable remission. Generalized skin whitening is neither an established clinical endpoint nor a supported claim.
